::::: {.panel-tabset}

## Stage 1 (public data)

::: {.overview_summary}

This stage uses public data - combination of ambsys, trust reports, and reported data in literature. It is a model of whole system. it can be used to ask:

How do changes in total vehicle hours, number of incidents per day, and/or handover delays affect Category 2 mean response time and resource utilisation?

:::

### Conceptual model

:::: {.overview_step}

### Incident arrives

**Distribution:** Homogeneous Poisson.

**Data:** Mean inter-arrival time by C1-C4.

**Source:** AmbSYS (derived from monthly incident counts).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true" title="More details"}

These are based on AmbSYS data, which reports total count of incidents for each response category (C1, C2, C3, C4) for each region for each month (A8, A10, A11, A12).

This can be converted to a mean inter-arrival time in minutes by dividing the minutes in that month by the number of incidents.

A Homogeneous Poisson Process (HPP) is used as we don’t have any information on incidents by day of week, which would be necessary for Non-Homogeneous Poisson Process (NHPP), which is most common in the literature.

:::

::::

::: {.overview_arrow}

↓

:::

:::: {.overview_step}

### Wait for resource

**Queue** First In First Out (FIFO).

**Resource:** 24/7 fixed pool.

**Data:** Number of ambulances.

**Source:** SWASFT Annual Report (derived from reported weekly conveying resource hours).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true" title="More details"}

A FIFO queue is a simple approach, common in the ambulance DES literature.

The number of ambulances is based on the [SWAST Annual Report and Accounts (1 April 2024 - 31 March 2025)](https://www.swast.nhs.uk/download/swasft-annual-report-and-accounts-202425pdf.pdf?ver=2868&doc=docm93jijm4n2818.pdf) section 3.4 Operational Resourcing which reports the weekly conveying resource hours. since April 2024, the mean was 52,000 per week.

Our model will assume a constant fleet size, with a fixed 24/7 resource pool with no shift pattern. One always-available ambulance provides 168 hours of capacity per week (24 × 7), so we approximate the number of ambulances as `resource_hours_per_week / 168`.

:::

::::

::: {.overview_arrow}

↓

:::

:::: {.overview_step}

### Response time (mobilisation time + time to scene)

**Distribution:** Lognormal.

**Data:** Mean and standard deviation by C1-C4.

**Source:** AmbSYS (derive reported mean and 90th percentile response time).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"  collapse="true" title="More details"}

These are based on **AmbSYS** data, which reports the mean and 90th percentile response time by response category (C1, C2, C3, C4) for each region for each month (A25, A26, A31, A32, A34, A35, A37, A38).

We use a lognormal distribution, as likewise implemented in [AmbModelOpen](https://github.com/nhsengland/AmbModelOpen/), who use empirical or lognormal distributions to model time to scene (tts).

Lognormal requires mean and standard deviation, so the standard deviation was estimated from the mean and 90th percentile, assuming a lognormal distribution.

:::

::::

::: {.overview_arrow}

↓

:::

:::: {.overview_step}

### On-scene time

**Distribution:** N/A - deterministic.

**Data:** Mean.

**Source:** Reported times from a study in London in 2023.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"  collapse="true" title="More details"}

The most relevant public data identified for on-scene time is a study from @davis_what_2025 in London, reporting times from 2023. For on-scene times, they report:

* Mean on-scene time: 44 minutes
* Median on-scene time: 46 minutes
* Inter-quartile range (IQR) for on-scene time: 33 to 54 minutes

Currently, the on-scene time is deterministic.

Ideally, these would be modelled using a lognormal distribution (as in [AmbModelOpen](https://github.com/nhsengland/AmbModelOpen/), who use empirical or lognormal for time at scene (tas)).

It may be possible though to estimate a SD from the provided mean/median/IQR, allowing use of a lognormal distribution.

:::

::::

::: {.overview_arrow}

↓

:::

:::: {.overview_step}

### Travel to hospital

**Distribution:** Exponential.

**Data:** Mean.

**Source:** Very rough estimate, based on reported distribution skew and average distance between where a person lives and an emergency hospital site as reported 2011 study data.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"  collapse="true" title="More details"}

The most relevant public data identified to support this estimate was @roberts_focus_2014. Two relevant sections of their report:

* **Left-skewed distribution** for distances between person's home and site where they received an emergency inpatient admission in 2011/12 (for whole of England) (Figure 3.2).
* **Average 12.24km (7.61 miles) in South West** between where a person lives and the hospital site used for an emergency admission.

No relevant data was identified to estimate travel speed, so an arbitrary speed of 45mph was chosen. Based on this, the average travel time to hospital would be:

* `7.61 miles / 45mph = 0.169 hours`
* `0.169 x 60 = 10.1 minutes`

Hence, a very rough mean time of 10 minutes is used, with an exponential distribution (as this is left skewed and only requires a mean).

Ideally, these would be modelled using a lognormal distribution (as in [AmbModelOpen](https://github.com/nhsengland/AmbModelOpen/), who use empirical or lognormal for time to site (ttsi)).

:::

::::

::: {.overview_arrow}

↓

:::

:::: {.overview_step}

### Handover

**Distribution:** Lognormal.

**Data:** Mean and SD.

**Source:** AmbSYS (derived from mean and 90th percentile handover time).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"  collapse="true" title="More details"}

This is based on **AmbSYS** data, which reports the mean and 90th percentile handover time overall for each region each month (A142, A143).

:::

::::

::: {.overview_arrow}

↓

:::

:::: {.overview_step}

### Wrap-up time

**Distribution:** N/A - deterministic.

**Data:** Mean.

**Source:** Reported wrap-up times in 2023 in London.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"  collapse="true" title="More details"}

The most relevant public data identified for on-scene time is a study from @davis_what_2025 in London, reporting times from 2023. For wrap up times, they report:

* Mean handover-to-clear time: 14 minutes

Currently, the wrap-up time is deterministic.

Ideally, these would be modelled using a lognormal distribution (as in [AmbModelOpen](https://github.com/nhsengland/AmbModelOpen/), who use empirical or lognormal for time to clear (ttc)).

:::
